title: Two Scars and a Quiet Valve / Tissue, Not Metal: Different Anticoagulation

blocks.text: Two Scars and a Quiet Valve / Tissue, Not Metal: Different Anticoagulation

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-11 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease (2025); SDCEP Antibiotic Prophylaxis Against Infective Endocarditis, implementation advice (2026); ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis (2023); NICE CG64 Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis (published 17 March 2008; last updated 8 July 2016) · Related AMaC: AMaC mechanical aortic valve and aortic stenosis stations; this one tests a tissue valve and the vein-graft scars
The patient is a man of 71, a retired surveyor. He had heart surgery four months ago and attends for review. Please examine his cardiovascular system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A sternotomy scar, a leg vein-harvest scar and a quiet soft murmur with no metallic click mean bypass grafts and a tissue valve. The anticoagulation is not the lifelong warfarin of a mechanical valve.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates see the sternotomy, call it a mechanical valve and advise lifelong warfarin to a high INR. Pass: no click, so tissue valve; aspirin or warfarin for the first three months, with aspirin continuing for his bypass grafts. Fail: lifelong warfarin at the mechanical target.

rows: Think
Say
Do
He has two kinds of scar. Look for both, and for a click, before you decide what is inside.
"May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; hands, face, pulse, JVP; chest wall and both legs.
Listen for what is absent: no metallic click. Then grade the flow murmur.
"I'm going to feel your chest, listen over the heart, and lean you forward."
Apex; thrill; four areas; carotids; lean forward in held expiration; lung bases; ankles; leg scar; cover him; clean hands.
Say the operations, say it is a tissue valve, and give the anticoagulation plan.
"He has had bypass grafts and a tissue aortic valve replacement. His anticoagulation differs from a mechanical valve."
Present in order; diagnosis; why not mechanical; antithrombotic plan; endocarditis advice; thank him.

Welfare
Starts without consent; presses on the healing scar; leaves him exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about scar pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone, keeps exposure to the minimum, and pauses if he tires.
R2
A
Systematic technique
Disorganised; omits the legs, pulse or one auscultation area.
Hands, pulse, JVP, chest wall, apex, four auscultation areas, carotids, lung bases, ankles and the leg scar.
Also leans him forward in held expiration and checks the teeth.
R3
B
Identifying signs
Reports a metallic click, or misses a scar.
Finds a sternotomy scar, a left leg vein-harvest scar, a soft ejection systolic murmur at the aortic area and no click.
Also finds normal heart sounds, no diastolic murmur, no failure, and no endocarditis signs.
R4
D
Differential diagnosis
Calls it a mechanical valve, or aortic stenosis that was never treated.
Coronary artery bypass grafting and a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement.
Also says why not mechanical: no metallic click, and a soft flow murmur is expected.
R5
E
Antithrombotic plan
Advises lifelong warfarin at a mechanical-valve INR, as if the valve were metal.
Says aspirin or warfarin to an INR of 2.5 for about 3 months, with aspirin continuing for his bypass grafts, and no lifelong warfarin unless another reason exists.

Also says atrial fibrillation would keep him on an anticoagulant: a DOAC is generally preferred; in the first 3 months after surgery the choice is a specialist decision; if warfarin is used, the usual target INR is 2.5.
R6
E
Endocarditis and follow-up
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): says a prosthetic valve needs no endocarditis precautions, or says nothing about endocarditis.

Says a prosthetic valve puts him in a high-risk group: dental hygiene and regular checks, antibiotic prophylaxis before the dental procedures his dentist and cardiologist advise, and echocardiographic follow-up.
Also says fever needs blood cultures before antibiotics, and that a tissue valve can degenerate over time.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: comfortable at rest; respiratory rate 14; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 138/76; SpO2 97% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Hands: no splinter haemorrhages. JVP not raised. Healed median sternotomy scar; left leg: long healed scar on the medial calf and thigh. Apex beat not displaced; no thrill. First sound normal; soft ejection systolic murmur at the right second space, not radiating; second sound soft; no click; no diastolic murmur. Lungs clear. No oedema. Teeth good.

Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. What operations has he had? (D) Told: surgery four months ago. 3. How do you know the valve is not mechanical? (D) 4. What anticoagulation does he need? (E) 5. What would you tell him about infection? (E)

Curveballs: He develops atrial fibrillation: he needs an anticoagulant; a DOAC is generally preferred (ESC/EACTS 2025); in the first 3 months after surgery the choice is a specialist decision; if warfarin is used, the usual target INR is 2.5. He has a fever: blood cultures first. How long will the valve last? Tissue valves can wear; echo follow-up.
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and asks about scar pain (G)
Inspects the chest and both legs for scars (A)
Listens for a click and for murmurs at four areas, leaning him forward (A)
Finds the sternotomy and leg scars and a soft flow murmur with no click (B)
States no failure and no endocarditis signs (B)
Names bypass grafting and a bioprosthetic aortic valve (D)
Says why it is not a mechanical valve (D)
Gives a limited warfarin or aspirin plan, not lifelong high-INR warfarin (E)
Advises dental hygiene, high-risk status for endocarditis with antibiotic prophylaxis before listed dental procedures, and blood cultures before antibiotics for fever (E)
Covers him, cleans hands and thanks him (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Sit back. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Looks at the chest scar only.) [R2 Fail] There's a metallic click. [R3 Fail] It's a mechanical valve. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Anticoagulation?
CANDIDATE: Warfarin for life, INR 3.0. [R5 Fail] No need to worry about infection. [R6 Fail]

Examiner note: Lifelong warfarin at a mechanical-valve INR raises the bleeding risk without need, and ignoring endocarditis is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail) because a prosthetic valve is a high-risk site. No consent, the leg scar missed, and a click invented.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your heart? Does the scar hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, pulse, JVP, chest wall, apex, four areas, carotids, bases, ankles, left leg.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: There is a sternotomy scar, a left leg vein-harvest scar, and a soft ejection systolic murmur at the aortic area, with no click. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: What has he had?
CANDIDATE: Coronary artery bypass grafting and a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Anticoagulation?
CANDIDATE: Aspirin or warfarin to an INR of 2.5 for about 3 months; his aspirin continues for the bypass grafts; no lifelong warfarin unless another reason exists. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Infection?

CANDIDATE: He now has a prosthetic valve, so he is at high risk of endocarditis: good dental hygiene and regular checks, antibiotics before the dental procedures his dentist and cardiologist advise, and echo follow-up. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not explain why it is not mechanical, the atrial fibrillation option or the blood cultures rule.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) May I examine your heart? Would you like a chaperone? I'll keep you covered and stop if you tire. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, pulse, JVP, scars, apex, four areas; leans him forward in held expiration; bases; ankles; teeth.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Sternotomy and left leg scars; normal heart sounds; soft ejection systolic murmur, no click, no diastolic murmur; no failure or endocarditis signs. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands, thanks him.) [R1 High]
EXAMINER: What has he had?
CANDIDATE: Bypass grafts and a tissue aortic valve; not mechanical because there is no metallic click and a soft flow murmur is expected. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Anticoagulation?

CANDIDATE: Aspirin or warfarin INR 2.5 for 3 months, and aspirin continues for the grafts. If he develops atrial fibrillation he needs an anticoagulant; a DOAC is generally preferred, the choice in the first 3 months after surgery is a specialist decision, and if warfarin is used the usual target INR is 2.5. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Infection?

CANDIDATE: High-risk group for endocarditis: dental hygiene, regular checks, prophylaxis before the dental procedures SDCEP lists, and tell any doctor or dentist about the valve. Fever needs blood cultures before antibiotics. Tissue valves can degenerate, so echo follow-up. [R6 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, teeth, the reason it is not mechanical, the atrial fibrillation option, cultures before antibiotics and valve durability.
R3: Reporting a metallic click. A tissue valve is quiet, and the invented sign leads to the wrong valve.
R4: Calling it mechanical. The missing click and the soft flow murmur say tissue, and the whole anticoagulation plan follows from this.
R5: Lifelong warfarin at a mechanical-valve INR. A tissue valve does not need it, and he takes bleeding risk for no benefit.
R6: Ignoring endocarditis, or saying no precautions are needed. A prosthetic valve puts him in a high-risk group, and he needs the advice and prophylaxis before listed dental procedures.
"Let me listen for a click again before I decide which valve it is."
"I hear no click, so I'd reconsider: this is a tissue valve."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"
Bioprosthetic valves are quiet: a soft flow murmur, no metallic click. A sternotomy scar with a leg vein-harvest scar suggests bypass grafting, with or without a valve.

Surgical bioprosthetic aortic valve without another anticoagulant indication: low-dose aspirin or warfarin should be considered for the first 3 months (an INR of 2.5 is the usual target; ESC/EACTS 2025 gives no target for this row); lifelong aspirin afterwards is optional for the valve alone, but he needs it for his bypass grafts. With atrial fibrillation he needs an anticoagulant: a DOAC is generally preferred; in the first 3 months after surgery the choice is a specialist decision; if warfarin is used, the usual target INR is 2.5. Mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin; direct oral anticoagulants are not used (ESC/EACTS 2025 recommends a VKA only).

Endocarditis: a surgically implanted prosthetic valve, tissue or mechanical, is a high-risk condition. SDCEP (2nd edition, March 2026), adapted from the ESC guideline, recommends antibiotic prophylaxis before specified dental procedures in high-risk people; NICE CG64 advises oral health, symptom awareness and caution with tattoos and piercing.
THINK: Two scars, no click: bypass and a tissue valve.
SAY: "Bypass grafting and a bioprosthetic aortic valve."
DO: Look at both legs; listen for a click.
NUMBERS: Aspirin or warfarin for 3 months (usual INR 2.5; ESC/EACTS 2025 gives none), then aspirin for the grafts; prosthetic valve: high-risk for endocarditis (SDCEP 2026).
TRAP: Lifelong high-INR warfarin; no endocarditis cover.
FINISH: Dental prophylaxis advice; cultures before antibiotics; echo follow-up.

2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease. Eur Heart J 2025;46(44):4635 (published online 29 August 2025). https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194 Supports: antithrombotic strategy after bioprosthetic and mechanical valve implantation (Recommendation Table 16).

SDCEP. Antibiotic Prophylaxis Against Infective Endocarditis: implementation advice, 2nd edition (March 2026). https://www.antibioticprophylaxis.sdcep.org.uk/ Supports: prosthetic valves as a high-risk group; prophylaxis before listed dental procedures.
2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis. Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948-4042. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193 Supports: prosthetic valve as a high-risk group; prevention advice.

NICE CG64. Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis (published 17 March 2008; last updated 8 July 2016). https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg64 Supports: advice on oral health, symptoms, tattoos and piercing for people at increased risk.
